gap_rows: Share of the full-period alpha earned on these days
Survival of the alpha with point-in-time betas
sentences: The halves and calendar years are fixed in advance. If you search for the year or split date that looks best, the p-values stop meaning what they say: with 10 years to choose from, the best year has a nominal p below 0.05 about 40% of the time even when nothing changed.
A year within two noise standard deviations of zero is ordinary for a stock with no alpha.
With thousands of days these tests detect even small departures. A rejection makes intervals approximate, not wrong.
A descriptive count, not a test.
Pure noise with this volatility typically falls about −17.5%.
Peak 22 Dec 2025, trough 12 Jan 2026, recovered 19 May 2026.
Second-half alpha minus first-half alpha: −8.7% a year (p = 0.477).
2 of 2 separate one-year windows show an alpha different from zero, after correcting for testing 2 windows.
The line compounds daily. It sits below the residual return in the table by about half the residual variance a year (0.6% here).

tooltips.Residual return, a year: What the stock earned per year beyond its factor exposures, alpha included. In-sample it equals the regression alpha exactly.
tooltips.t-statistic: Distance of the residual return from zero in standard errors. Between −2 and 2 (p above 0.05), you cannot tell it from zero.
tooltips.Residual volatility, a year: How much the stock moves for reasons the five factors do not explain. Higher volatility makes alpha harder to measure.
tooltips.Residual Sharpe (information ratio): Residual return per unit of residual risk. Do not compare it with a total-return Sharpe. 0.5 for 10 years is only about 1.6 standard errors.
tooltips.Cumulative (compounded): What the daily-rebalanced paper hedge compounded to, before costs.
tooltips.Compound growth, a year: Lower than the residual return by about half the residual variance a year. Shown beside the arithmetic values, never added to them.
tooltips.Hit rate: Share of days the residual was positive. Near 50% is normal; it says how often, not how much.
tooltips.Max drawdown: Worst fall of the cumulative residual line from a previous high.
tooltips.Skew: Below 0: rare large residual losses. Above 0: rare large gains, often earnings days.
tooltips.Excess kurtosis: Above 0: more extreme days than a normal distribution. Intervals here are then approximate.
